original_question: Because Painleve equations are integrable and are solvable by the isomonodromy method through an associated Riemann-Hilbert problem, how can that structure be used to build software for computing Painleve solutions numerically, including combining asymptotic information from the Riemann-Hilbert problem with efficient numerical codes to evaluate solutions at finite values of the independent variable?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Open Problem 4.1, second bullet, read together with the immediately preceding technical question in the section: how to use the Painlevé equations' isomonodromic/Riemann–Hilbert structure in developing numerical software, specifically by combining asymptotic information from the Riemann–Hilbert problem with efficient numerical computation at finite z.
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the correct open problem and captures its central ingredients very faithfully: the Painlevé equations are treated as integrable equations; the relevant integrable structure is the isomonodromy method via an associated Riemann–Hilbert problem; the goal is software for numerical study/computation; and the nearby contextual sentence in Section 4 explicitly asks how to combine asymptotic information from the Riemann–Hilbert problem with efficient numerical codes to compute the solution at finite values of the independent variable. This is also consistent with the shorter summary of the same problem in the introduction.
missing_details: The paper frames this as Open Problem 4.1, specifically its second bullet, not as a general question about all integrable systems or all nonlinear ODEs.
The scope is the Painlevé equations and their solutions (Painlevé transcendents) in general, not one specific equation or one special family of solutions.

The nearby Section 4 context writes the dependent variable as w(z) and the computational target as evaluating w(z) at finite values of z; your draft refers only generically to the independent variable.
The paper places this question inside a broader numerical-software agenda: it asks for reliable, easy-to-use software for studying the Painlevé equations numerically.
Section 4 explicitly contrasts this goal with standard ODE solvers, especially Runge–Kutta methods, and asks whether one can do better for integrable equations such as the Painlevé equations.

The paper treats two neighboring issues as separate bullets in Open Problem 4.1: improving on Runge–Kutta methods, and whether to use integrable discretizations via discrete Painlevé equations. Those are adjacent but distinct from the specific Riemann–Hilbert/software question.

No extra algebraic data such as ambient ring, degree, homogeneity, or nilpotency conditions are part of this problem; the missing information is about computational scope, notation, and the exact numerical target.
refined_question: Can one develop reliable, easy-to-use numerical software for studying solutions w(z) of the Painlevé equations that explicitly exploits their integrable isomonodromic structure—namely, the associated Riemann–Hilbert problem—by combining asymptotic information extracted from that Riemann–Hilbert formulation with efficient numerical schemes so as to compute the Painlevé transcendents accurately at finite values of z, preferably improving on standard Runge–Kutta-type ODE solvers?
justification: The paper's nearest official formulation is not a theorem or conjecture but the second bullet of Open Problem 4.1 in Section 4. Your draft is already very close to that official statement and additionally incorporates, almost verbatim, the immediately preceding contextual sentence about combining asymptotic Riemann–Hilbert information with efficient numerical codes at finite z. The introduction gives a shorter summary of the same target. The refined version therefore stays narrow: it keeps the focus on Painlevé equations, numerical software, and the use of isomonodromy/Riemann–Hilbert structure, while adding the paper's explicit notation w(z), finite-z objective, and the contrast with standard Runge–Kutta methods. There is no explicitly proved equivalent reformulation in the paper, so none should be added.
